tamil:
பொச்சாப்பார்க் கில்லை புகழ்மை அதுஉலகத்து
எப்பால்நூ லோர்க்கும் துணிவு.
transliteration:
Pochchaappaark killai pukazhmai adhuulakaththu
Eppaalnoo lorkkum thunivu.
current_meaning: Careless, forgetful people never win lasting fame. The writers of every kind of book in the world agree on this.
elementary: Ask a coach, a music teacher, a doctor, or a chef, and they will all tell you the same thing: people who keep forgetting and not paying attention never become great at anything. When everyone agrees on something, it's worth listening!
university: புகழ்மை means ‘the state of having fame’, and துணிவு here means a settled conclusion, not courage. Parimelazhagar takes எப்பால் நூலோர் to mean the authors of treatises of every kind, not only of polity (நீதி நூல்). He explains that the rule holds for everyone, not only kings: anyone pursuing any of the four aims of life (aṟam, poruḷ, iṉpam, vīṭu) will fail if heedless, and so will have no fame. Pavanar agrees that the rule is universal but argues that உலகம் here means the Tamil world and that எப்பால் நூல் refers to the branches of Tamil learning, much of which has since been lost; he points out that Valluvar does not say the northern (Sanskrit) texts agree. Manakkudavar reads the couplet simply as saying that heedlessness brings no fame. Parimelazhagar groups 533-535 as describing the harm (ஏதம்) that comes to the heedless.

tamil:
அச்ச முடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை ஆங்கில்லை
பொச்சாப் புடையார்க்கு நன்கு.
transliteration:
Achcha mutaiyaarkku aranillai aangillai
Pochchaap putaiyaarkku nanku.
current_meaning: A fort is no use to someone who is a coward at heart. In the same way, no advantage is any use to someone who is careless.
elementary: A castle with tall walls won't help a guard who is too scared to stand at his post. And a house full of good locks won't help if you forget to lock the door. What really protects you is what's going on inside your own head.
university: The couplet is built on a simile (உவமை) marked by ஆங்கு (‘in the same way’). Fear inside makes outer defences (அரண்) useless, and forgetfulness inside makes outer goods (நன்கு) useless. Parimelazhagar spells out the அரண் as forest, mountain and similar strongholds, and glosses நன்கு as wealth of every kind, called ‘the good’ because it is a means to good. His conclusion is that just as the stronghold of the fearful falls, the riches of the heedless perish. Pavanar adds armies to the list of advantages and derives நன்கு from நல் > நன். Manakkudavar sums the couplet up as saying that the heedless have no protection. By pairing அச்சம் (fear) with பொச்சாப்பு (heedlessness), Valluvar treats both as inner failures of a ruler's mind that no outward resource can make up for.

tamil:
முன்னுறக் காவாது இழுக்கியான் தன்பிழை
பின்னூறு இரங்கி விடும்.
transliteration:
Munnurak kaavaadhu izhukkiyaan thanpizhai
Pinnooru irangi vitum.
current_meaning: Someone who carelessly fails to guard against trouble before it comes will be sorry for their own mistake when the trouble hits.
elementary: If you know a test is coming and you don't study, you'll feel terrible when you see questions you can't answer. Getting ready before trouble comes is much better than feeling sorry afterwards.
university: முன் உற (‘before it arrives’) and பின் ஊறு (‘when the blow has fallen’) frame the couplet in time, and இழுக்கியான் (‘one who slipped, was negligent’) is described by காவாது (‘without guarding’). Parimelazhagar says the troubles in view are those that can be guarded against, namely what enemies do when they spot a lapse. He treats ஊறு as standing for ஊற்றின்கண், with both the case-ending and the linking syllable dropped, and explains இரங்கிவிடும் as ‘will be left to grieve’, because once the trouble has come it can no longer be warded off. Pavanar widens the preventable troubles to include famine and flood, and takes விடும் in the sense of ‘perishing’. Manakkudavar's gloss is almost word for word the same as Parimelazhagar's. This couplet closes Parimelazhagar's group of three (533-535) on the harm that comes to the heedless.

tamil:
இழுக்காமை யார்மாட்டும் என்றும் வழுக்காமை
வாயின் அதுவொப்பது இல்.
transliteration:
Izhukkaamai yaarmaattum endrum vazhukkaamai
Vaayin adhuvoppadhu il.
current_meaning: If a person can stay alert and careful toward everyone and at all times, nothing else is as good as that.
elementary: Being careful once is easy. Being careful with everyone, every day, even when things are going great, is the real superpower. If you can do that, it's better than almost any other gift you could have.
university: The couplet plays on two near-synonyms: இழுக்காமை (‘not slipping’, that is, unforgetfulness) must be present வழுக்காமை (‘without a lapse’). Parimelazhagar explains யார்மாட்டும் as reaching even the king's own people, the servants who do his work and his kin, and என்றும் as meaning ‘in days of growth and of decline alike’. He parses வாயின் as a conditional form built on the verbal-noun stem வாய் (‘to come right, to fall into place’). Pavanar adds that வழுக்காமை means applying this without fail in every task, and he explicitly rejects Parimelazhagar's analysis of வாயின், citing Tolkāppiyam and Kural 737 to argue that வாய் is an intransitive verb. Manakkudavar reads the couplet as a rule for the careful administration of justice. Together with 537, this couplet forms Parimelazhagar's pair on the excellence of unforgetfulness.

tamil:
அரியஎன்று ஆகாத இல்லைபொச் சாவாக்
கருவியால் போற்றிச் செயின்.
transliteration:
Ariyaendru aakaadha illaipoch chaavaak
Karuviyaal potrich cheyin.
current_meaning: No job is too hard, however difficult people say it is, if you do it carefully, with a mind that never forgets or slips.
elementary: Building a huge Lego castle sounds impossible. But if you keep the picture in your head, follow each step carefully, and don't lose track, you can finish it. A mind that doesn't forget is like a super-tool that makes hard jobs possible.
university: அரிய என்று ஆகாத இல்லை is a double negative: ‘there is nothing that, being called difficult, cannot be done’. Parimelazhagar takes பொச்சாவாக் கருவி to mean ‘the unforgetting mind’. On his reading, பொச்சாவாத has lost its final syllable by poetic licence, and the mind is called கருவி (‘instrument’) because it is the inner instrument (அந்தக்கரணம்); போற்றிச் செயின் means ‘if one does it with careful thought’. His summary is that people with unbroken attention and sound planning accomplish everything easily. Pavanar calls this gloss over-learned and prefers to read பொச்சாவாக் கருவி as an appositional compound, ‘the instrument that is unforgetfulness’. Manakkudavar likewise glosses it as மறவாமையாகிய கருவி. Modern commentators such as Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah reflect both readings.

tamil:
புகழ்ந்தவை போற்றிச் செயல்வேண்டும் செய்யாது
இகழ்ந்தார்க்கு எழுமையும் இல்.
transliteration:
Pukazhndhavai potrich cheyalventum seyyaadhu
Ikazhndhaarkku ezhumaiyum il.
current_meaning: Do carefully the things that wise people have praised. Those who ignore them and leave them undone will find no good in any of their seven births (the many lives a person is believed to live).
elementary: Your teachers and parents tell you some things are really worth doing, like being kind, doing homework, and telling the truth. Knowing that isn't enough; you have to actually do them. People who shrug those things off miss out on good things again and again.
university: புகழ்ந்தவை means ‘the things praised’. Parimelazhagar identifies them as the duties that works on polity single out as proper to kings: the three powers, the four expedients (upāya), the five kinds of action, the six policies, and so on. இகழ்ந்தார் here does not mean ‘those who scorned’; all the commentators take it as ‘those who neglected or forgot’, and Parimelazhagar glosses it as மறந்தவர். He reads எழுமையும் இல் as ‘no good in all seven births’, on the ground that those who fall away from their proper duty reap only suffering in hell, and he treats எழுமை (‘sevenfoldness’) as a metonymy. Pavanar rejects Parimelazhagar's appeal to caste duty (சாதி தருமம்) as foreign to the text, lists instead celebrated deeds of the ancient Tamil kings as examples of ‘praised acts’, and reads எழுமை as a conventional number. Parimelazhagar says this couplet sets out what must be done without forgetting.

tamil:
இகழ்ச்சியின் கெட்டாரை உள்ளுக தாந்தம்
மகிழ்ச்சியின் மைந்துறும் போழ்து.
transliteration:
Ikazhchchiyin kettaarai ulluka thaandham
Makizhchchiyin maindhurum pozhdhu.
current_meaning: Whenever you feel full of pride and pleased with yourself, remember the people who were ruined because they got careless.
elementary: When you win a prize and feel like the best in the world, it's a good moment to remember the story of the hare who was so sure of winning that he took a nap and lost to the tortoise. Remembering other people's mistakes keeps you careful.
university: இகழ்ச்சி here means heedless disregard (it shares a root with இகழ்ந்தார் in 538), and மைந்துறும் போழ்து means ‘the moment one grows strong or elated’. Parimelazhagar makes kings the subject: when they grow confident in their own pleasures, they should remember those of old who perished through the lapse such pleasure breeds. He explains that the text says ‘their own delight’ because the king owns the means of pleasure, and that it ties elation to ruin because neglect and downfall arise together. The point, he says, is that one who recalls the ruined will think ‘I too shall perish that way’ and will not grow elated. He also records a variant reading, எண்ணுக for உள்ளுக, which Pavanar attributes to Manakkudavar. Manakkudavar gives the couplet a concrete application: kings should have their food, clothing and unguents examined, that is, guard against poisoning.

tamil:
உள்ளியது எய்தல் எளிதுமன் மற்றுந்தான்
உள்ளியது உள்ளப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Ulliyadhu eydhal elidhuman matrundhaan
Ulliyadhu ullap perin.
current_meaning: It is easy to reach your goal, as long as you keep your mind fixed on it from then on.
elementary: If you want to learn to ride a bike, you have to keep that goal in your mind every day, even after you fall. Kids who keep thinking about their goal and don't let it slip away usually get there.
university: The couplet turns on repeating உள்ளியது (‘what was thought of’) together with the verb உள்ளு (‘to think of, keep in mind’): attaining your aim is easy if you can ‘think again what you thought’. Parimelazhagar reads it as advice to a king: he will easily obtain what he intended, exactly as he intended it, if he can keep thinking of that same thing, which he explains as striving towards it without forgetting. He takes மன் as an ஒழியிசை particle, one that implies an unspoken ‘but that is hard to manage’, so the couplet quietly admits that sustained attention is the difficult part. Pavanar rejects this analysis of மன் as unsuitable here and takes மற்று to mean ‘afterwards, further’. Manakkudavar reads the couplet as the requirement to remember, above all, what one first resolved. Parimelazhagar groups 539-540 as the means (உபாயம்) for achieving unforgetfulness.

tamil:
ஓர்ந்துகண் ணோடாது இறைபுரிந்து யார்மாட்டும்
தேர்ந்துசெய் வஃதே முறை.
transliteration:
Orndhukan Notaadhu Iraipurindhu Yaarmaattum
Therndhusey Vaqdhe Murai.
current_meaning: Justice means looking into every case carefully, favoring no one, being fair to all, and then thinking it through before acting.
elementary: Imagine a teacher who finds two kids fighting over a broken toy. A fair teacher doesn’t just blame the kid she likes less. She asks questions, listens to both, thinks it over, and then decides. Even if the one who broke it is her favourite helper, the rule is the same for him. That is what “doing it the right way” means.
university: This opening couplet works as a definition: முறை (justice, right order) is a four-step procedure. ஓர்ந்து means investigating what offence was committed; கண்ணோடாது means without கண்ணோட்டம், the soft favour that comes from familiarity or affection (Valluvar gives this quality its own chapter, 58, where it is praised in private life, which is why it has to be ruled out here); இறைபுரிந்து is glossed by Parimelazhagar as holding to impartiality (இறை = நடுவுநிலைமை), though some modern readers take இறை as ‘the ruler’ and the phrase as ‘the king, wishing it’; and தேர்ந்து செய்வது means deciding with those learned in the law books and then giving the fitting penalty. யார்மாட்டும் (‘with anyone at all’) governs the whole sequence, so a kinsman gets no exemption. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah follow this procedural reading; Kalaignar compresses it to ‘not leaning to either side’. Parimelazhagar notes that the chapter follows பொச்சாவாமை (vigilance) and comes before its opposite, கொடுங்கோன்மை (Ch. 56); செங்கோல், the ‘straight sceptre’, is the standard Tamil metonym for just rule. ytamizh and Thirukkural.net give the same text.

tamil:
வானோக்கி வாழும் உலகெல்லாம் மன்னவன்
கோல்நோக்கி வாழுங் குடி.
transliteration:
Vaanokki Vaazhum Ulakellaam Mannavan
Kolnokki Vaazhung Kuti.
current_meaning: All living things on earth look up to the sky for rain. In the same way, the people of a country look to their king’s fair rule in order to live.
elementary: Plants in a garden wait for rain, and without it they dry up. The people of a country are a bit like that garden: they are waiting for their leaders to be fair and kind. When the leader rules well, it is like a good rain, and everyone grows.
university: The couplet is built on an exact parallel: வான் நோக்கி வாழும் உலகு (the world that lives looking to the sky) matches கோல் நோக்கி வாழும் குடி (the citizenry that lives looking to the sceptre). As commentators note, வான் here stands for rain by metonymy, which echoes the opening chapter on rain (வான்சிறப்பு, Ch. 2), where rain sustains all life. Parimelazhagar reads உலகெல்லாம் as ‘all living beings’ and குடி as the settled subjects of the kingdom. Just as he reads கோல் throughout the chapter, the sceptre means just rule, not simply power. Varadarasan and Pappaiah keep the rain comparison; Kalaignar makes it ‘good government is as necessary to citizens as rain is to living things’. The comparison already hints at 545 and 559 (in the next chapter), where just rule and rainfall are causally linked. Both sources agree on the text; வாழுங் is the sandhi form of வாழும் before குடி.

tamil:
அந்தணர் நூற்கும் அறத்திற்கும் ஆதியாய்
நின்றது மன்னவன் கோல்.
transliteration:
Andhanar Noorkum Araththirkum Aadhiyaai
Nindradhu Mannavan Kol.
current_meaning: A king’s fair rule is what holds up the holy books of the learned priests and the dharma (the right way of living) that those books teach.
elementary: Think of a town library. The books are wonderful, but if nobody keeps the doors safe and the roof mended, the books get ruined and people stop reading. A fair ruler is like the person who keeps the library safe, so that good teachings and good behaviour can last.
university: Parimelazhagar takes அந்தணர் நூல் as the Vedas and அறம் as the dharma they lay down, and he explains ஆதியாய் நின்றது (‘stood as the origin’) causally: if the sceptre fails, the Veda is forgotten and dharma lapses, so the sceptre is their support, not their source in time. Varadarasan follows him (‘the scripture revered by the Brahmins’). Modern commentators widen the terms: Solomon Pappaiah reads அந்தணர் as ‘those who cultivate wisdom’ and நூல் as their books of knowledge, Kalaignar speaks of ‘the books of the virtuous’, and Sivayogi Sivakumar reads அந்தணர் as ‘those who know the end’. The couplet sets out a characteristic Kural view: learning and morality are not self-sustaining; they need a just political order to protect them. Pope’s ‘Learning and virtue of the sages spring / From all-controlling sceptre of the king’ overstates the idea of origin. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
குடிதழீஇக் கோலோச்சும் மாநில மன்னன்
அடிதழீஇ நிற்கும் உலகு.
transliteration:
Kutidhazheeik Kolochchum Maanila Mannan
Atidhazheei Nirkum Ulaku.
current_meaning: The whole world holds on to the feet of a great king who rules with love and keeps his people close.
elementary: A team captain who looks after every player, helping the slow ones and cheering up the scared ones, ends up with a team that would follow her anywhere. People hold on to a leader who holds on to them first.
university: The couplet turns on a chiasmus of the verb தழுவு (embrace), used twice in the lengthened form தழீஇ: the king embraces the people (குடி தழீஇ), and the world embraces his feet (அடி தழீஇ). The long vowel (இசைநிறை அளபெடை) fills out the metre and gives the word emphasis. கோல் ஓச்சுதல், ‘wielding the sceptre’, is the idiom for ruling. Parimelazhagar explains ‘embracing the subjects’ as protecting them with love and learning what they lack; ‘clinging to his feet’ means the world will not leave him, so his kingdom stands firm. Varadarasan: ‘the world holds fast to the feet of the king who rules embracing his people with love’. Pappaiah turns it into people living ‘around the feet’ of such a ruler, and Kalaignar has the whole earth honouring the footsteps of a good government. In சுற்றந்தழால் (Ch. 53) Valluvar used the same verb for embracing kin; here the embrace is extended to the whole people. The text is the same in both sources.

tamil:
இயல்புளிக் கோலோச்சும் மன்னவன் நாட்ட
பெயலும் விளையுளும் தொக்கு.
transliteration:
Iyalpulik Kolochchum Mannavan Naatta
Peyalum Vilaiyulum Thokku.
current_meaning: In the country of a king who rules by fair law, the seasonal rains come and the harvests are rich, both together.
elementary: When a family shares fairly and nobody grabs, dinner time is happy and there is enough for everyone. The old Tamil poets believed a whole country works that way: when the ruler is fair, even the rain and the crops seem to join in.
university: இயல்புளி is இயல்பு with the instrumental ending உளி (= ஆல்), ‘by the proper nature/way’. Parimelazhagar glosses it as ruling according to the method laid down in the books of statecraft (நீதிநூல்), and Varadarasan (‘நீதி முறைப்படி’) and Pappaiah (‘அரச நீதிநூல்கள் கூறியபடி’) follow him. நாட்ட is a genitive plural predicate, ‘belong to his land’. பெயல் is seasonal rainfall and விளையுள் the abundant yield. The final தொக்கு (having gathered together) means the two are always found together there. Behind the couplet lies a belief found across ancient cultures, that the king’s righteousness governs the fertility of the land. Valluvar states the negative in the next chapter: முறைகோடி மன்னவன் செய்யின் உறைகோடி ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல் (559). Kalaignar reads it as a simile, that just government is like timely rain bringing a good harvest, which softens the causal claim. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
வேலன்று வென்றி தருவது மன்னவன்
கோலதூஉங் கோடா தெனின்.
transliteration:
Velandru Vendri Tharuvadhu Mannavan
Koladhooung Kotaa Thenin.
current_meaning: A king wins not by his spear but by his scepter (his rule), as long as that rule stays straight and fair.
elementary: A kid who wins a game by cheating doesn’t really win, because soon nobody wants to play with him. A kid who plays fair keeps her friends and keeps winning. For a ruler too, being fair is stronger than being scary.
university: The couplet sets வேல் (spear, the emblem of military force) against கோல் (sceptre, the emblem of justice), two words that differ by a single consonant. அதூஉம், the lengthened form of அதுவும் (‘that too’, with அளபெடை), adds a condition: the sceptre gives victory only if it too does not bend (கோடாது எனின்). The verb கோடு, ‘to bend, be crooked’, is the root of கொடுங்கோல் (tyranny, Ch. 56). Parimelazhagar explains that the spear wins only because the subjects stand loyally with a just king, so victory really comes from the sceptre and the spear is its instrument. Varadarasan and Pappaiah agree; Kalaignar makes the contrast explicit: not the spear that fells enemies, but the unbending sceptre that lets the people live. The point anticipates the chapters on the army (77–78), which treat military strength as dependent on the loyalty that just rule creates. The text is the same in both sources.

tamil:
இறைகாக்கும் வையகம் எல்லாம் அவனை
முறைகாக்கும் முட்டாச் செயின்.
transliteration:
Iraikaakkum Vaiyakam Ellaam Avanai
Muraikaakkum Muttaach Cheyin.
current_meaning: The king protects the whole world, and justice protects the king, as long as he never fails to do justice.
elementary: If you always tell the truth and treat your friends fairly, then when someone spreads a nasty rumour about you, your friends stand up for you. Your fairness becomes your shield. It works the same way for rulers.
university: The two halves mirror each other with the verb காக்கும் (guards): இறை காக்கும் வையகம் எல்லாம் (the lord guards the whole world) and அவனை முறை காக்கும் (justice guards him). The condition முட்டாச் செயின், ‘if he does it without lapse’ (முட்டு = obstruction, failure), is the hinge. Parimelazhagar explains that the merit of just rule protects the king from harm that would otherwise come to him; Varadarasan: ‘if he rules without harming justice, that justice itself protects him’. Pappaiah reads முட்டா as qualifying முறை, i.e. ‘his flawless, upright rule protects him’. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads the condition oddly (‘even if they err’), which the grammar does not support. The idea is the political counterpart of the Aram principle that dharma protects those who protect it; compare Manu’s ‘dharmo rakṣati rakṣitaḥ’. Both sources give the same text.

tamil:
எண்பதத்தான் ஓரா முறைசெய்யா மன்னவன்
தண்பதத்தான் தானே கெடும்.
transliteration:
Enpadhaththaan Oraa Muraiseyyaa Mannavan
Thanpadhaththaan Thaane Ketum.
current_meaning: A king whom people cannot easily reach, and who does not look into their problems and give fair judgments, will fall low and be ruined, even without an enemy.
elementary: Imagine a class monitor who locks herself away and never listens when kids come to her with a problem. Problems pile up, everyone gets upset, and soon nobody trusts her. She didn’t need an enemy to lose her job. She lost it all by herself.
university: எண்பதம் means ‘easy access’ (எண் = easy, பதம் = occasion or audience; Varadarasan: எளிய செவ்வி); தண்பதம் means a ‘low state’ (Parimelazhagar: தாழ்ந்த நிலை). The two rhyming compounds frame the couplet. Commentators take the negation of ஓரா (not examining) and முறைசெய்யா (not doing justice) as extending back over எண்பதத்தான், so the king is one who is not accessible, does not investigate, and does not give justice; Pope accordingly renders ‘Hard of access, nought searching out’. Pappaiah keeps the positive reading grammatically but gives the same sense. தானே கெடும் (‘perishes of himself’) is taken by Parimelazhagar and Varadarasan to mean ‘even without enemies’ (பகைவரில்லாமலும்): neglect of justice is self-destruction. Kalaignar departs and reads எண்பதம் as pomp or display. The couplet links accessibility to justice, a theme taken up again in வெருவந்தசெய்யாமை (Ch. 57). The text is the same in both sources.

tamil:
குடிபுறங் காத்தோம்பிக் குற்றம் கடிதல்
வடுவன்று வேந்தன் தொழில்.
transliteration:
Kutipurang Kaaththompik Kutram Katidhal
Vatuvandru Vendhan Thozhil.
current_meaning: Protecting the people from outside harm, caring for them, and punishing crime is not a fault in a king. It is his proper job.
elementary: A lifeguard who blows her whistle at kids running by the pool isn’t being mean. It is her job, keeping everyone safe. A fair ruler who stops people from doing wrong is doing the same kind of job.
university: Parimelazhagar separates two kinds of protection: புறம் காத்து, guarding the people from others (enemies, robbers, grasping officials), and ஓம்பி, protecting them from himself (for example, by not over-taxing). Only then comes குற்றம் கடிதல், removing crime by fitting punishment. வடு அன்று (‘not a scar or blemish’) answers an implied objection that punishment, as a form of harm, conflicts with the ethic of non-injury taught in the Aram section (e.g. Ch. 32–33); வேந்தன் தொழில் (‘the king’s work’) makes it a duty of office. Varadarasan follows Parimelazhagar closely. Pappaiah reads குற்றம் as the people’s grievances (குறைகள்), which shifts the emphasis from punishment to redress. Kalaignar adds that the ruler should punish whoever the offender is, without fearing reproach. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads புறம் as ‘beyond the borders’. The couplet prepares for the harsher 550. The text is the same in both sources.

tamil:
கொலையிற் கொடியாரை வேந்தொறுத்தல் பைங்கூழ்
களைகட் டதனொடு நேர்.
transliteration:
Kolaiyir Kotiyaarai Vendhoruththal Paingoozh
Kalaikat Tadhanotu Ner.
current_meaning: When a king punishes cruel killers with death, it is like a farmer pulling out weeds to protect the young crop.
elementary: A gardener pulls out weeds not because she hates plants but because the weeds would choke the vegetables. The Kural says a ruler must stop people who seriously hurt others, so that everyone else can grow up safe. (Grown-ups still argue about how harsh such punishments should be.)
university: The final couplet puts the chapter’s argument about punishment in an agricultural image: பைங்கூழ் is the young green crop, and களை கட்டல் is weeding. The phrase கொலையிற் கொடியாரை is read in two ways. Varadarasan and Pappaiah take கொலையின் as instrumental, so the king punishes the cruel ‘by death’ (கொலைத்தண்டனையால்). Kalaignar takes it as the offence, so the cruel are ‘those who commit murder and similar cruelties’. Parimelazhagar’s commentary follows the first line of reading and presents capital punishment as the protection of the good, just as the weed is removed for the crop’s sake. Commentators note the tension with the Aram section’s உயிர் கொல்லாமை (not killing, Ch. 33). The usual resolution is that Aram states the individual’s ethic while Porul states the king’s duty. Modern readers such as Kalaignar keep the metaphor but stress that it applies to hardened offenders, not the ordinary wrongdoer. The next chapter, Tyranny, reverses the image. The text is the same in both sources.

tamil:
கொலைமேற்கொண் டாரிற் கொடிதே அலைமேற்கொண்டு
அல்லவை செய்தொழுகும் வேந்து.
transliteration:
Kolaimerkon daarir kodithe alaimerkondu
Allavai seythozhukum vendhu.
current_meaning: A king who keeps hurting his people and keeps doing unjust things is crueler than a person who kills for a living.
elementary: Picture a playground bully who knocks you over once, and then picture a class monitor who is supposed to look after everyone but pushes kids around every single day. The monitor is worse, because the hurt never stops and the one person meant to protect you is the one hurting you. Valluvar says a cruel king is like that monitor, only much bigger.
university: The chapter is the mirror image of the preceding one, செங்கோன்மை (the straight sceptre, ch. 55): கொடுங்கோல் is the ‘bent’ rod of a ruler who governs by oppression. The key word அலை means harassing or tormenting, and Parimelazhagar glosses அலைமேற்கொண்டு as taking up, out of covetousness for wealth (பொருள்வெஃகி), the business of harassing the subjects. His reason for the comparison is that the murderer’s harm lasts a moment, whereas the tyrant’s is lifelong, so ‘harassment is crueller than killing’. He also notes the grammatical point that வேந்து, a neuter-class noun, is used here of a person (திணை/பால் மயக்கம்). Manakkudavar gives substantially the same reading, while Solomon Pappaiah stresses greed for the people’s property. The text is uniform across ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net and thirukkural.com; the older continuous text on thirukkural-thamizh.org shows the unsplit sandhi forms யலைமேற்கொண் / டல்லவை.

tamil:
வேலொடு நின்றான் இடுவென் றதுபோலும்
கோலொடு நின்றான் இரவு.
transliteration:
Velodu nindraan iduven rathupolum
Kolodu nindraan iravu.
current_meaning: When a king demands money from his people, it is like a robber with a spear standing on a lonely road and saying, “Give it to me.”
elementary: If a big kid holding a stick says ‘Can I please have your lunch?’, it isn’t really a question, because you know what happens if you say no. Valluvar says that when a king with power over you ‘asks’ for extra money, it is the same as a robber demanding it.
university: The image is of the solitary highwayman (வேலொடு நின்றான்) and the king ‘standing with the rod’ (கோலொடு நின்றான்), the rod here meaning the power to punish (ஒறுத்தல் தொழில்). Parimelazhagar draws two inferences: ‘standing with a spear’ implies the robber is alone on a deserted road, and the word இரவு (begging, request) shows that what the king asks for is not the lawful revenue (இறைப்பொருள் அன்மை). Because the king’s request carries an unspoken threat to punish anyone who refuses, even ‘asking’ becomes tyranny; he adds that kurals 551-552 together state the fault of tyranny itself. Manakkudavar reads கோலொடு நிற்றல் as standing in the posture of one who administers justice, and adds that even a voluntary-seeming levy above the fixed dues is like robbery on the road. Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar take the couplet as a comment on extortionate taxation. The text is the same across the sources consulted.

tamil:
நாடொறும் நாடி முறைசெய்யா மன்னவன்
நாடொறும் நாடு கெடும்.
transliteration:
Naadorum naadi muraiseyyaa mannavan
Naadorum naadu kedum.
current_meaning: A king who does not look into wrongs every day and give fair judgments will watch his country grow weaker every day.
elementary: If you never look after a garden, weeds creep in a little each day until the flowers are gone. A king who doesn’t check every day for unfair things happening, and fix them, lets his whole country slowly go to ruin in the same way.
university: The couplet plays on நாள் / நாடு: நாடொறும் (daily, from நாள் + தொறும்) and நாடி (examining, from நாடு-தல்), then நாடு (country). Parimelazhagar glosses: the king who does not daily examine the wrongs occurring in his land and render fitting justice will daily ‘lose’ his country. He explains that since the country is a limb (உறுப்பு) of the king, the verb ‘perish’ is attributed to him, and that ‘losing’ here means failing to enjoy its fruits (பயன் எய்தாமை). He records an alternative construal, ‘the king’s country perishes daily’ (மன்னவன் நாடு நாள்தொறும் கெடும்), which Manakkudavar and Kalaignar adopt. For the first word, thirukkural.com prints the unassimilated form நாள்தொறும், while ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net give the sandhi form நாடொறும்.

tamil:
கூழுங் குடியும் ஒருங்கிழக்கும் கோல்கோடிச்
சூழாது செய்யும் அரசு.
transliteration:
Koozhung kudiyum orungizhakkum kolkodich
Choozhaathu seyyum arasu.
current_meaning: A king who twists justice and acts without thinking about what will happen will lose both his riches and his people at once.
elementary: Imagine a lemonade stand owner who cheats customers without thinking ahead. Soon the customers stop coming, and with them goes the money. Valluvar says a careless, unfair king loses his treasure and his people together, because the people are where the treasure comes from.
university: கூழ் (literally gruel or food) stands for wealth, and குடி for the subjects. Parimelazhagar makes the pairing precise: கூழ் is the wealth already amassed, and குடி is the people who are the source of wealth yet to be earned, so the tyrant loses past and future income together. சூழாது means ‘without deliberating’ on what will follow, and கோல்கோடி means ‘bending the sceptre’; he notes கோடி stands for the infinitive கோட. He adds that the next couplet gives the cause of losing wealth already amassed. Manakkudavar marks this couplet as stating the fault that comes from acting without deliberation. Kalaignar reads குடி more loosely as ‘the people’s esteem’. The text is the same across the sources consulted, and Pope’s rendering ‘who counsel doth refuse’ follows the sense of சூழாது.

tamil:
அல்லற்பட்டு ஆற்றாது அழுதகண் ணீரன்றே
செல்வத்தைத் தேய்க்கும் படை.
transliteration:
Allarpattu aatraathu azhuthakan neerandre
Selvaththaith theykkum padai.
current_meaning: The tears of people who are suffering more than they can bear are a weapon that wears away a cruel king’s riches.
elementary: Water dripping on a stone for a long, long time can wear a hole right through it. Valluvar says the tears of people treated unfairly are like that water: drop by drop, they wear away the riches of the ruler who made them cry.
university: அல்லல் is distress, ஆற்றாது ‘unable to bear it’, and படை ‘army’ or ‘weapon’. The verb தேய்க்கும் (wears away, grinds down) has led translators to render படை as a file or saw (Pope has ‘sharp instruments’, and the prose translation ‘a saw’). Parimelazhagar calls the figure ஏகதேச உருவகம் (partial metaphor): Valluvar does not say ‘the tree of wealth’, but the verb implies it. He explains that the destructive work really done by the sin of causing suffering is credited to the tears that are its sign, ‘because nothing is crueller than those tears’, and that the sense is that the wealth wastes away quickly. He groups kurals 553-556 as stating the evils that befall the tyrant himself. The text is the same across the sources consulted.

tamil:
மன்னர்க்கு மன்னுதல் செங்கோன்மை அஃதின்றேல்
மன்னாவாம் மன்னர்க் கொளி.
transliteration:
Mannarkku mannuthal sengonmai akhthindrel
Mannaavaam mannark koli.
current_meaning: Fair rule is what makes a king’s fame last. Without it, his glory will not stay.
elementary: A trophy you won by cheating doesn’t feel like yours, and people stop cheering once they find out. Valluvar says a king’s glory is like that: only fair, honest rule keeps it shining, and without fairness it fades away.
university: The couplet repeats the root மன்- ‘to endure’ for effect: மன்னர் (kings), மன்னுதல் (enduring) and மன்னா (will not endure). ஒளி (light, lustre) means renown. Parimelazhagar supplies the instrumental case lost by elision: ‘kings’ fame endures by the straight sceptre’. He cites Nāṉmaṇikkaṭikai 17 (‘if you wish to endure in this world, plant fame’) to show that fame is what makes a person endure. He explains the plural (ஒளி taken as many forms of fame, from victory, generosity and so on) and concludes that if their fame does not last, the kings themselves do not last. Some continuous-text editions read the sandhi form அஃதின்றேன் and மன்னாவா மன்னர்க் for அஃதின்றேல் மன்னாவாம். Manakkudavar puts this couplet first in the ‘faults’ series, taking the loss of glory as the first penalty of misrule.

tamil:
துளியின்மை ஞாலத்திற்கு எற்றற்றே வேந்தன்
அளியின்மை வாழும் உயிர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Thuliyinmai gnaalaththirku etratre vendhan
Aliyinmai vaazhum uyirkku.
current_meaning: A king without kindness is to his people what a lack of rain is to the earth.
elementary: When it doesn’t rain for a long time, plants wilt, rivers shrink, and animals go thirsty. A king without kindness makes his people wilt in just the same way, because his care is like rain to them.
university: துளி (a drop) stands for rain by synecdoche. Parimelazhagar says the word was chosen because a drop is the most telling part of rain. அளி means gracious, tender care, and உயிர் (life, living beings) here stands for the subjects. The construction எற்று… அற்றே (‘of what kind…? just so’) makes a rhetorical comparison. Parimelazhagar notes that this couplet puts negatively what kural 542 had said positively: the whole world lives looking to the sky for rain, and the subjects look to the king’s sceptre. He groups kurals 557-558 as stating the evils that fall on those who live in the tyrant’s land. Solomon Pappaiah reads அளி more broadly as ‘righteous governance’. The text is the same across the sources consulted.

tamil:
இன்மையின் இன்னாது உடைமை முறைசெய்யா
மன்னவன் கோற்கீழ்ப் படின்.
transliteration:
Inmaiyin innaathu udaimai muraiseyyaa
Mannavan korkeezhp padin.
current_meaning: Under an unfair king, having money brings more misery than having nothing at all.
elementary: Imagine a class where a mean monitor takes the best toy from anyone who brings one. Soon, the kids who bring nice toys are the most worried ones. Valluvar says that under a greedy king, being rich becomes more dangerous than being poor.
university: The paradox turns on இன்மை (having nothing) and உடைமை (possessing). Parimelazhagar explains it by describing what the covetous king does: those who own property are the ones who suffer seizures, torture and binding ‘till the hands ache’ (கைந்நோவ யாப்புண்டல்), so under such a ruler wealth is worse than poverty. He applies it to everyone (யாவர்க்கும்), not just the rich, and groups kurals 557-558 as stating the evils that fall on those who live in the tyrant’s land. Manakkudavar agrees (‘even the wealthy suffer’) and counts 557-559 as the evils of failing to do justice. கோற்கீழ்ப் படின் means ‘if one falls under the sceptre’. The text is the same across the sources consulted.

tamil:
முறைகோடி மன்னவன் செய்யின் உறைகோடி
ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல்.
transliteration:
Muraikodi mannavan seyyin uraikodi
Ollaathu vaanam peyal.
current_meaning: If a king rules unfairly, the seasons go wrong and the clouds will not give rain.
elementary: Think of a team captain who cheats. Soon nobody plays well, the whole game falls apart, and it feels as if even luck has left. The old poets said that when a king is unfair, even the rain stops coming on time.
university: The couplet repeats கோடி (bending): the king ‘bends’ justice (முறைகோடி) and the rain ‘bends’ from its season (உறைகோடி). Parimelazhagar notes that both forms stand for the infinitive கோட, glosses உறைகோடுதல் as ‘failing to rain at the time for rain’, and says the cause is given in the next couplet. Classical commentators take this as a real cosmic link between royal righteousness and the monsoon, a belief widespread in Indian thought. Kalaignar instead reads உறை as reservoirs and rain-storage works that fall to ruin under misrule, so the rain cannot be stored and used. The text is the same across the sources consulted, apart from sandhi spacing in the older continuous text (செய்யி னுறைகோடி யொல்லாது).

tamil:
ஆபயன் குன்றும் அறுதொழிலோர் நூல்மறப்பர்
காவலன் காவான் எனின்.
transliteration:
Aapayan kundrum aruthozhilor noolmarappar
Kaavalan kaavaan enin.
current_meaning: If the ruler does not protect the land, the cows give less milk and the learned priests who do the six sacred duties forget their holy books.
elementary: If a school has no one looking after it, the lunch kitchen stops working and the teachers stop teaching. Soon both food and learning are gone. Valluvar says that when a king doesn’t protect his land, food (milk from cows) and learning (the old books) both start to fade.
university: ஆபயன் is ‘the yield of the cow’ (ஆ, cow, and பயன், fruit), meaning milk and its products. அறுதொழிலோர் are ‘those of the six duties’, which Parimelazhagar lists as the Brahmin’s six duties: studying, teaching, sacrificing, officiating at sacrifice, giving and receiving (ஓதல், ஓதுவித்தல், வேட்டல், வேட்பித்தல், ஈதல், ஏற்றல்). He ties the couplet to 559: without milk there is no oblation (அவி), without recitation there are no mantras, so sacrifice stops, and so the rain fails. He groups 559-560 as the evils that befall the tyrant’s land. Modern commentators widen the reference: Solomon Pappaiah reads ‘the wise’ (ஞானியர்), and Kalaignar and Sivayogi Sivakumar read ‘productive work and the major occupations decline’. The older continuous text has the sandhi form நூன்மறப்பர்.

tamil:
தக்காங்கு நாடித் தலைச்செல்லா வண்ணத்தால்
ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது வேந்து.
transliteration:
Thakkaangu naadith thalaichchellaa vannaththaal
Oththaangu oruppadhu vaendhu.
current_meaning: A true king looks into a wrong fairly and carefully, then punishes it in a way that fits the crime, so that it does not happen again.
elementary: Imagine a teacher who finds a broken window. A good teacher first finds out calmly who did it and why, and then gives a fair consequence, not too big and not too small, so it won't happen again. This kural says a good ruler works the same way: find out the truth first, then correct fairly.
university: The chapter title வெருவந்த செய்யாமை means ‘not doing things that cause dread (veru)’, and Valluvar opens it not by forbidding punishment but by defining its right form. Three steps are packed into the couplet: தக்காங்கு நாடி (investigating as is fitting, i.e., impartially), ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுத்தல் (punishing in a measure that matches the offence), and the purpose clause தலைச்செல்லா வண்ணத்தால் (so that the wrong does not advance or recur). The traditional commentators, with Parimelazhagar at their head, read this as the positive standard against which the tyranny of the previous chapter (கொடுங்கோன்மை, ch. 56) is measured, and modern glosses (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) all stress neutrality in inquiry and proportion in penalty. The definition-style ending ‘… வேந்து’ (‘that is a king’) makes proportionate justice constitutive of kingship itself. Text agrees across ytamizh.com and thirukkural-thamizh.org, the latter printing the older sandhi-joined form (வண்ணத்தா / லொத்தாங் கொறுப்பது) with no change in wording.

tamil:
கடிதோச்சி மெல்ல எறிக நெடிதாக்கம்
நீங்காமை வேண்டு பவர்.
transliteration:
Kadidhoachchi mella eriga nedidhaakkam
Neengaamai vaendu bavar.
current_meaning: Rulers who want their good times to last should raise the stick sternly but bring it down gently. They should warn firmly but punish mildly.
elementary: Think of a parent who says in a serious voice, ‘If you do that again, there will be no TV for a month!’, but when it happens, takes away TV for just one evening. The warning is strong, the punishment is gentle. The kural says leaders who do this keep their people’s trust for a long time.
university: The image is of a raised stick: கடிது ஓச்சி (lift it high, severely) but மெல்ல எறிக (bring it down softly). The classical commentary, followed by Mu. Varadarasanar, reads this as appearing to proceed with great severity while in fact not exceeding due measure, while Kalaignar’s modern gloss separates the stages as stern reproof but mild punishment. The reward named is நெடிது ஆக்கம் நீங்காமை, prosperity that does not depart for a long time, so the couplet argues from prudence as much as from mercy. Pope’s ‘raise the rod with brow severe, but let it gently fall’ has become the standard English rendering. thirukkural-thamizh.org prints the sandhi form ‘மெல்ல வெறிக’, which is the same words as ‘மெல்ல எறிக’.

tamil:
வெருவந்த செய்தொழுகும் வெங்கோல னாயின்
ஒருவந்தம் ஒல்லைக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Veruvandha seydhozhugum vengoalan aayin
Oruvandham ollaik kedum.
current_meaning: A cruel king who keeps doing things that fill his people with fear will surely and quickly be ruined.
elementary: Imagine a team captain who yells and scares everyone all the time. Soon nobody wants to play for them, and the team falls apart. The kural says a ruler who keeps people frightened will quickly lose everything.
university: This couplet supplies the chapter’s title phrase: வெருவந்த செய்து ஒழுகும் describes a ruler whose habitual conduct (ஒழுகுதல், ongoing practice) is to do dread-inducing things. வெங்கோலன், the ‘hot’ or cruel sceptre, is the opposite of the செங்கோல் (straight sceptre) of chapter 55. ஒருவந்தம் means ‘certainly, without doubt’ and ஒல்லை ‘quickly’, so the prediction is doubly emphatic: sure and soon. Commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) agree in glossing ‘veru’ as the fear felt by the subjects (குடிகள் அஞ்சும்படி). The couplet is read identically in both sources consulted.

tamil:
இறைகடியன் என்றுரைக்கும் இன்னாச்சொல் வேந்தன்
உறைகடுகி ஒல்லைக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Iraikadiyan endruraikkum innaachchol vaendhan
Uraikadugi ollaik kedum.
current_meaning: A king whose people call him “our cruel ruler” will have his life cut short and will quickly be destroyed.
elementary: If everyone at school whispers ‘the new class monitor is mean,’ that monitor won’t be monitor for long. The kural says when a whole country calls its king cruel, his time is almost up.
university: The couplet turns from the ruler’s acts to the people’s verdict: இறை கடியன் (‘the lord is harsh’) is the இன்னாச் சொல், the painful word, that the subjects speak. The ruler is thus defined by his reputation, and public opinion becomes a political force. உறை கடுகி is glossed by Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘his lifespan shrinking’ (ஆயுள் குறைந்து), while Pappaiah reads it as the term of his rule contracting; both readings fit, and Pope’s ‘his age shall dwindle’ follows the first. ஒல்லைக் கெடும் repeats the ‘swiftly perishes’ of 563, binding the two couplets together. The text is the same in both sources.

tamil:
அருஞ்செவ்வி இன்னா முகத்தான் பெருஞ்செல்வம்
பேஎய்கண் டன்னது உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Arunjevvi innaa mugaththaan perunjelvam
Paeey kandannadhu udaiththu.
current_meaning: The great riches of a ruler who is hard to meet and who greets people with an angry face are like treasure guarded by a demon. They are scary and help no one.
elementary: Imagine a huge toy box that belongs to someone who never opens the door and scowls at everyone who knocks. Nobody gets to play with the toys, so it’s as if a monster were sitting on them. The kural says a leader who can’t be reached and always frowns makes his riches useless.
university: Two faults are named: அருஞ்செவ்வி, rare or difficult audience (செவ்வி = an opportune moment of access), and இன்னா முகம், a disagreeable countenance. The simile பேஎய் கண்டு அன்னது is read in the commentarial tradition as wealth that a pēy (demon, ghoul) has seen or seized: it exists but inspires only fear and benefits no one, which is why Pope renders ‘blasted by demon’s glance’ and Pappaiah ‘held by a bhūta’. The couplet widens the chapter’s idea of dread from punishment to everyday demeanour: an unapproachable, scowling ruler terrifies without lifting a rod. The spelling பேஎய் preserves the classical alapedai (vowel prolongation) for metre, and both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
கடுஞ்சொல்லன் கண்ணிலன் ஆயின் நெடுஞ்செல்வம்
நீடின்றி ஆங்கே கெடும்.
transliteration:
Kadunjollan kannilan aayin nedunjelvam
Needindri aangae kedum.
current_meaning: If a ruler speaks harshly and shows no kindness, his great riches will not last. They will disappear right then.
elementary: A shopkeeper who is rude and never smiles at customers soon has an empty shop, no matter how many goods are on the shelves. The kural says a leader with harsh words and no kindness loses even great riches very quickly.
university: கடுஞ்சொல்லன் is one given to harsh words, and கண்ணிலன், literally ‘eyeless’, means lacking kaṇṇōṭṭam, the gracious, considerate regard that is the subject of the very next chapter (58, கண்ணோட்டம்). The couplet thus bridges two chapters: without kindly regard, even நெடுஞ்செல்வம் (vast, long-accumulated wealth) perishes நீடின்றி ஆங்கே, without delay, on the spot. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses கண்ணிலன் as கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாதவன் and Pappaiah as lacking முகதாட்சண்யம் (considerateness), while Kalaignar renders it as a ‘merciless heart’. The contrast நெடும் (long) and நீடு இன்றி (without lasting) is a deliberate verbal play. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
கடுமொழியும் கையிகந்த தண்டமும் வேந்தன்
அடுமுரண் தேய்க்கும் அரம்.
transliteration:
Kadumozhiyum kaiyigandha thandamum vaendhan
Adumuran thaeykkum aram.
current_meaning: Harsh words and punishments that go too far are like a file that slowly wears down a king’s power to beat his enemies.
elementary: A metal file rubs a little bit off a key every time you use it, until one day the key no longer works. The kural says that every cruel word and every too-big punishment rubs away a little of a leader’s strength, until it is gone.
university: கையிகந்த தண்டம் is punishment that has ‘gone beyond the hand’, exceeding its proper limit (Mu. Varadarasanar: முறைகடந்த தண்டனை). அடுமுரண் is the destroying strength, the capacity to crush enemies, and அரம் is a file, so the metaphor is of gradual erosion rather than sudden collapse, complementing the ‘swift ruin’ of 563–566. The couplet echoes 566 (harsh words) and 561 (proportionate punishment), making excess, not punishment itself, the target. The word தண்டம் (Sanskrit daṇḍa) links Valluvar to the wider Indian daṇḍanīti tradition of measured punishment. thirukkural-thamizh.org prints the sandhi form ‘அடுமுரண் டேய்க்கு மரம்’, identical in wording.

tamil:
இனத்தாற்றி எண்ணாத வேந்தன் சினத்தாற்றிச்
சீறிற் சிறுகும் திரு.
transliteration:
Inaththaatri ennaadha vaendhan sinaththaatrich
Seeril sirugum thiru.
current_meaning: A king who does not think things through with his advisers, and then gets angry and blames them, will see his good fortune shrink.
elementary: Imagine a group leader who never asks the team for ideas, and then, when the project goes wrong, shouts at everyone. The team stops helping, and things get worse and worse. The kural says a leader who skips advice and then explodes in anger loses what they have.
university: The couplet is syntactically compact and has two established readings. Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah take இனத்து ஆற்றி எண்ணாத as ‘not deliberating together with his circle (ministers)’, so the fault is failure to consult followed by angry outbursts; Pope, following the older commentary, reads it as handing affairs to ministers without himself reflecting, and then raging at them when things fail. On either reading the pattern is the same: neglect of counsel, then சினத்து ஆற்றி சீறுதல், being carried along by anger and flaring at subordinates. The result is that திரு (Śrī, royal fortune) சிறுகும், dwindles. Here ‘dread’ is directed at the king’s own ministers, extending the chapter’s concern from subjects to the inner court. The text is the same in both sources.

tamil:
செருவந்த போழ்திற் சிறைசெய்யா வேந்தன்
வெருவந்து வெய்து கெடும்.
transliteration:
Seruvandha poazhdhil siraiseyyaa vaendhan
Veruvandhu veydhu kedum.
current_meaning: A king who has not built a safe place of defense ahead of time will be filled with fear when war comes, and will quickly be destroyed.
elementary: If you never build a shelter and a big storm comes, you get frightened and soaked. The kural says a ruler who doesn’t prepare protection in peaceful times panics and falls when trouble arrives.
university: சிறை here means a protective barrier or fortification (Mu. Varadarasanar: அரண்), not ‘prison’ in the modern sense; the couplet is about defence made ready before செரு (battle) arrives. The striking reversal is in வெருவந்து: the very dread (veru) the tyrant inflicted on others now falls on him, so the chapter’s key word turns back on its source. Commentators connect this to the preceding couplets: a king who has alienated his people through fear and cruelty lacks the human ‘fortress’ of their loyalty when danger comes, which is why this apparently military verse belongs in a chapter on not ruling by terror. வெய்து கெடும் means ‘perishes swiftly/painfully’. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
கல்லார்ப் பிணிக்கும் கடுங்கோல் அதுவல்லது
இல்லை நிலக்குப் பொறை.
transliteration:
Kallaarp pinikkum kadungoal adhuvalladhu
Illai nilakkup porai.
current_meaning: A cruel ruler who keeps ignorant, unlearned people as his helpers is the heaviest weight the earth has to carry. There is none heavier.
elementary: Picture a bully who gathers other kids who don’t know right from wrong to help him push everyone around. That gang makes the whole playground miserable. The kural says a cruel ruler with foolish helpers is the heaviest weight the world has to carry.
university: The closing couplet names the social mechanism of tyranny: கடுங்கோல் (the harsh sceptre) பிணிக்கும் (binds, attaches) கல்லார் (the unlearned) to itself, meaning it draws in and relies on men without learning or moral training to carry out its will. The traditional commentary, followed by Mu. Varadarasanar, Kalaignar, and Pope (‘Tyrants with fools their counsels share’), reads it this way; Pappaiah’s gloss instead stresses a regime that punishes so as to terrify, propped up by those who have not studied the books of justice. பொறை means a load or burden, and the idea of the earth (நிலம்) groaning under wicked rulers is widespread in Indian thought. The couplet ties back to chapter 41 (கல்லாமை, lack of learning) and closes the chapter by showing that terror is never exercised alone. thirukkural-thamizh.org prints the sandhi-joined ‘கடுங்கோ லதுவல்ல தில்லை’, identical in wording.

tamil:
கண்ணோட்டம் என்னும் கழிபெருங் காரிகை
உண்மையான் உண்டிவ் வுலகு.
transliteration:
Kannottam ennum kazhiperung kaarikai
Unmaiyaan undiv vulagu.
current_meaning: The world keeps going only because of a very great beauty called kannottam (looking at others with kindness and care).
elementary: Think of a playground where the big kids notice the little ones and help them up when they fall. That kind look makes the whole playground a happy place. Valluvar says the whole world keeps going because people, especially leaders, look at others kindly like that.
university: The chapter title கண்ணோட்டம் literally means ‘the running (ஓட்டம்) of the eye (கண்)’, i.e., the eye going out towards another in consideration; Parimelazhagar defines it as the disposition that, on seeing those one is familiar with, cannot bring itself to refuse or hurt them, and he places the chapter in the Arasiyal (royal) section as a quality of the king. The phrase கழிபெருங் காரிகை (‘exceedingly great beauty’) treats benignity as an ornament rather than a duty, a theme picked up again in kural 575. The second line, உண்மையான் உண்டு இவ்வுலகு (‘because of its existence, this world exists’), is a strong ontological claim: social order itself depends on this quality. Modern commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah) gloss it as ‘looking at a person’s face’ and softening accordingly, while Kalaignar reads it more broadly as love joined with compassion. The text agrees across ytamizh.com and thirukkural-thamizh.org, the latter printing the older sandhi-joined form (கண்ணோட்ட மென்னுங் … யுண்மையா னுண்டிவ்) with no change in wording.

tamil:
கண்ணோட்டத் துள்ளது உலகியல் அஃதிலார்
உண்மை நிலக்குப் பொறை.
transliteration:
Kannottath thulladhu ulagiyal aqdhilaar
Unmai nilakkup porai.
current_meaning: All the everyday business of the world runs on kindness toward others. People without it are just a burden on the earth.
elementary: Imagine a class where everyone shares pencils and helps each other. One child never helps anyone and only takes. The class works because of the helpers; the one who never helps just makes things heavier for everyone. Valluvar says people without kindness are like extra weight the earth has to carry.
university: உலகியல் means ‘the conduct or course of the world’, i.e., everyday social transactions, and Parimelazhagar takes the first line to mean that all such dealings are sustained by kannottam. The second line’s உண்மை (‘existence’, not ‘truth’ here) and பொறை (‘burden’) make a stark judgement: a person without kindly regard contributes nothing and simply weighs on the land, an image the Tamil tradition also uses of the ungrateful and the idle. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both render பொறை as சுமை/பாரம் (load), while Kalaignar stresses the ‘embracing with love’ that such people lack. The couplet thus moves from the cosmic claim of 571 to its negative corollary. ytamizh.com and thirukkural-thamizh.org agree; the latter prints the sandhi-joined form (துள்ள துலகிய லஃதிலா / ருண்மை).

tamil:
பண்என்னாம் பாடற்கு இயைபின்றேல் கண்என்னாம்
கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்.
transliteration:
Pan ennaam paadarku iyaipindrel kan ennaam
Kannottam illaadha kan.
current_meaning: What use is a tune that does not fit the song? In the same way, what use is an eye that shows no kindness?
elementary: If someone plays a happy tune while you sing a sad lullaby, the music doesn’t help at all; it just sounds wrong. Valluvar says eyes are the same: eyes are meant to look kindly, and eyes without kindness are like music that doesn’t match the song.
university: பண் is the technical term for a melodic mode in Tamil music (roughly comparable to a raga), and இயைபு means ‘concordance’ or ‘fitting together’; the couplet thus draws on the Tamil musical tradition, in which the right pann had to suit the song and its mood. Parimelazhagar explains that just as a pann not matched to its song is useless, an eye not joined to kannottam is useless, so kindness is the eye’s proper ‘accompaniment’. The rhetorical question என்னாம் (‘what will it be?’, i.e., of what use) is repeated to link the two halves. Solomon Pappaiah renders பண் as ராகம், and all four commentaries on ytamizh.com share this reading. thirukkural-thamizh.org has பண்ணென்னாம் … கியைபின்றேற் for ytamizh’s பண்என்னாம் … இயைபின்றேல், which are orthographic and sandhi differences only.

tamil:
உளபோல் முகத்தெவன் செய்யும் அளவினால்
கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்.
transliteration:
Ulapol mugaththevan seyyum alavinaal
Kannottam illaadha kan.
current_meaning: Eyes that show no proper kindness only seem to be there in the face. What else are they good for?
elementary: A doll can have beautiful painted eyes, but they never notice when you are sad. They are just there for decoration. Valluvar says eyes that never look kindly at anyone are like doll’s eyes: they are in the face, but they are not really doing an eye’s job.
university: உளபோல் (‘as if they exist’) makes the eyes a mere appearance on the face (முகத்து), and எவன் செய்யும் asks what use they serve. The key qualifier is அளவினால் (‘in due measure’): Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar read the kindness required as kannottam within proper limits, i.e., kindness that does not override duty, which anticipates kural 578. Solomon Pappaiah likewise speaks of ‘kannottam within bounds’ (வரம்பிற்கு உட்பட்ட), while Kalaignar reads it as the eyes failing to stir love and pity in the heart. The couplet shares its second line verbatim with 573 (கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்), a deliberate repetition that ties the two images together. thirukkural-thamizh.org prints உளபோன் … மளவினாற் (sandhi forms) for ytamizh’s உளபோல் … அளவினால், with no change in wording.

tamil:
கண்ணிற்கு அணிகலம் கண்ணோட்டம் அஃதின்றேல்
புண்ணென்று உணரப் படும்.
transliteration:
Kannirku anigalam kannottam aqdhindrel
Punnendru unarap padum.
current_meaning: Kindness is the jewel that makes the eye beautiful. Without it, the eyes will look like nothing more than two sores.
elementary: People wear necklaces and bracelets to look nice. Valluvar says the nicest thing your eyes can ‘wear’ is kindness. If your eyes are always angry or cold, people will not see pretty eyes at all; they will see something that hurts, like a scrape.
university: அணிகலம் (‘ornament, jewel’) recalls the காரிகை (‘beauty’) of 571: kannottam is the eye’s jewellery, not merely its function. The shocking alternative, புண் (‘wound, sore’), plays on the near-rhyme கண்/புண், and the passive உணரப்படும் (‘will be perceived as’) implies the judgement of others; Solomon Pappaiah specifies ‘by the wise’ (பெரியோரால்), as does the Pope/Drew-style English gloss on ytamizh. Parimelazhagar’s point is that eyes are honoured only because they carry grace; without it they are merely openings in the flesh. This is the couplet the chapter is most remembered for, and its imagery of ornament versus wound is found in later Tamil ethical literature. The two sources agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi forms கண்ணிற் கணிகலங் … மஃதின்றேற் / புண்ணென் றுணரப்.

tamil:
மண்ணோ டியைந்த மரத்தனையர் கண்ணோ
டியைந்துகண் ணோடா தவர்.
transliteration:
Mannodu iyaindha maraththanaiyar kannodu
iyaindhukan nodaa thavar.
current_meaning: People who have eyes but never look kindly at others are like trees standing in the ground. They have the shape but not the feeling.
elementary: A tree stands in one place and can’t notice when someone near it is crying. Valluvar says a person who has eyes but never looks kindly at others is just like that tree: standing there, but not really caring about anyone.
university: The couplet is built on a careful parallel: மண்ணோடு இயைந்த மரம் (‘a tree joined to the soil’) and கண்ணோடு இயைந்து கண்ணோடாதவர் (‘those who, though joined to eyes, do not let the eye run out [in kindness]’). The verb கண்ணோடு is the root of the chapter’s title, so the line plays on having கண் (eyes) but not doing கண்ணோட்டம். Parimelazhagar is usually cited as noting that trees too were said to have ‘eyes’ (buds or nodes), so that the unkind are no better than eyed trees; this pun is reported in commentary tradition and should be treated with some caution. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses ‘like a tree that has eyes but does not see’, while Solomon Pappaiah stresses that such people move about but are as insensible as a tree fixed in the earth. The two texts agree word for word, with the line break falling inside கண்ணோ / டியைந்து in both.

tamil:
கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லவர் கண்ணிலர் கண்ணுடையார்
கண்ணோட்டம் இன்மையும் இல்.
transliteration:
Kannottam illavar kannilar kannudaiyaar
Kannottam inmaiyum il.
current_meaning: People without kindness are really without eyes. And people who truly have eyes are never without kindness.
elementary: Imagine your friend drops their lunch and everyone looks away, but one kid runs over to help. Valluvar would say only that kid truly ‘saw’. Having real eyes means noticing people and caring about them; if you never care, it is as if you have no eyes at all.
university: The couplet is a chiasmus built on the single word கண்: those without கண்ணோட்டம் are கண்ணிலர் (‘eyeless’), and those who are கண்ணுடையார் (‘possessed of eyes’) are never without கண்ணோட்டம். Parimelazhagar reads it as a definition by convertibility: in the moral sense, having eyes and having kannottam are one and the same thing, so that physical sight without kindness does not count as sight. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah render it almost identically, while Kalaignar reverses the emphasis, saying the eyes of the compassionate alone deserve the name. With 576 it completes a sequence (573-577) that systematically strips the unkind eye of every value. Both sources agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has sandhi forms கண்ணோட்ட மில்லவர் … மின்மையு மில்.

tamil:
கருமம் சிதையாமல் கண்ணோட வல்லார்க்கு
உரிமை உடைத்திவ் வுலகு.
transliteration:
Karumam sidhaiyaamal kannoda vallaarkku
Urimai udaiththiv vulagu.
current_meaning: The world truly belongs to those who can show kindness without letting their duty be harmed.
elementary: A good referee is friendly and kind to all the players, but still calls a foul when someone breaks the rules. Valluvar says the best leaders are like that: kind to everyone, but they never let kindness stop them from doing what is right.
university: கருமம் here means one’s proper task, and for a king Parimelazhagar specifies it as the administration of justice (the ytamizh English gloss adds ‘administration of justice’ in brackets); சிதையாமல் means ‘without letting it be spoiled’. The couplet thus sets a limit on kannottam: kindness toward familiar people must never become favouritism that ruins just government, which explains the அளவினால் (‘in due measure’) of 574. உரிமை உடைத்து இவ்வுலகு (‘this world has rightful ownership [for them]’) promises that such rulers are the world’s natural possessors. Modern commentators generalise the principle to anyone who is compassionate without neglecting their duties (Kalaignar: ‘first in not failing duty and in showering mercy’). Both texts agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi forms கருமஞ் சிதையாமற் … வல்லார்க் / குரிமை யுடைத்திவ்.

tamil:
ஒறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பினார் கண்ணும்கண் ணோடிப்
பொறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பே தலை.
transliteration:
Oruththaatrum panbinaar kannum kannodip
Poruththaatrum panbe thalai.
current_meaning: The highest goodness is to show kindness and patiently put up with even those who like to hurt us.
elementary: If a classmate keeps being mean to you, the easy thing is to be mean back. Valluvar says the very best thing is to stay kind and patient with them anyway. That is the hardest kind of kindness, and so it is the greatest.
university: ஒறுத்து ஆற்றும் பண்பினார் means ‘those whose nature is to cause harm/afflict’, and the matching பொறுத்து ஆற்றும் பண்பு is ‘the nature that bears it and carries on’; the verbal rhyme ஒறுத்து/பொறுத்து sets the injurer’s nature against the forbearer’s. கண்ணும் (‘even towards’) extends kannottam from familiar friends to enemies, the chapter’s highest reach. Commentators differ slightly on the object: Mu. Varadarasanar reads ‘even those who deserve punishment’, stressing a judge’s leniency, while Solomon Pappaiah and the English gloss read ‘those who grieve or harm us’, stressing personal forbearance; Parimelazhagar’s royal reading allows both. தலை (‘head’, i.e., foremost) ranks this above all other forms of kindness. Both texts agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has கண்ணுங்கண் for ytamizh’s கண்ணும்கண்.

tamil:
பெயக்கண்டும் நஞ்சுண் டமைவர் நயத்தக்க
நாகரிகம் வேண்டு பவர்.
transliteration:
Peyakkandum nanjundu amaivar nayaththakka
Naagarigam vendu pavar.
current_meaning: People who want the kind of politeness everyone admires will even drink poison they watched a friend pour for them, and still stay friends.
elementary: Suppose a friend gives you a cookie that tastes awful, and you know they didn’t make it right. A very gracious person might eat it and still smile, because they care more about the friend than the cookie. Valluvar tells this as an extreme story to show how far true kindness can go.
university: The couplet is deliberately hyperbolic: பெயக் கண்டும் (‘even having seen it poured’) and நஞ்சு உண்டு அமைவர் (‘they drink the poison and remain calm/content’) describe people who knowingly accept harm from someone close rather than break the bond. நாகரிகம் here does not mean modern ‘civilisation’; Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar take it as the refined kannottam, the urbane courtesy that is நயத்தக்க (‘worthy of being desired’ by all). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah specify that the poison is offered by those one has long associated with, and the Sangam anthology Natrinai (poem 355) is frequently cited for the closely related idea that the truly refined will drink even poison offered by friends. Commentators treat the couplet as illustrating the extreme limit of kannottam rather than a literal instruction. Both texts agree word for word.

tamil:
ஒற்றும் உரைசான்ற நூலும் இவையிரண்டும்
தெற்றென்க மன்னவன் கண்.
transliteration:
Otrum uraisaandra noolum ivaiyirandum
Thetrenga mannavan kan.
current_meaning: A ruler should know that he has two eyes: his spies, who show him what is really happening, and the respected books of law, which show him what should be done.
elementary: A captain steering a ship needs two things: a lookout who shouts what he sees on the sea, and a map that shows the right route. With only one, the ship gets lost. This kural says a ruler is the same: he needs people who tell him what is really going on, and good rules that tell him what is right.
university: The chapter title ஒற்றாடல் means ‘the employment (ஆடல், handling) of spies’; one printed text glosses it ஒற்றரை ஆளும் திறம், ‘the skill of managing spies’. It follows directly on கண்ணோட்டம் (ch. 58, ‘the kindly eye’), and Valluvar continues the eye image by naming two organs of royal sight: ஒற்று (the spy, or intelligence generally) and உரைசான்ற நூல் (a treatise ‘full of renown’). Parimelazhagar takes the second to be the science of polity (நீதிநூல்), and the commentators draw the contrast that the treatise shows what should be done while the spy shows what is being done; a king lacking either is half-blind. The verb தெற்றென்க (‘let him know clearly’) turns the saying into a direct order. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read it the same way, and the text is identical on ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net and thirukkural-thamizh.org, the last printing it in older sandhi-joined form (ஒற்று முரைசான்ற நூலு மிவையிரண்டுந்).

tamil:
எல்லார்க்கும் எல்லாம் நிகழ்பவை எஞ்ஞான்றும்
வல்லறிதல் வேந்தன் தொழில்.
transliteration:
Ellaarkkum ellaam nigazhpavai enjnjaandrum
Vallaridhal vaendhan thozhil.
current_meaning: A king’s job is to find out quickly, at all times, everything that happens to everyone, whether they are enemies, friends, or neither.
elementary: A good school principal wants to know right away if someone is being bullied, if a pipe is leaking, or if a new student feels lost, not a month later. This kural says a ruler’s real work is the same: always finding out quickly what is happening to everyone.
university: The couplet stacks three universals, எல்லார்க்கும் (to all persons), எல்லாம் (all things) and எஞ்ஞான்றும் (at all times), then adds வல் (‘swiftly’) to அறிதல் (knowing). Parimelazhagar spells out ‘all persons’ as the king’s enemies, friends and neutrals (பகைவர், நட்பினர், நொதுமலர்), and Pappaiah and Kalaignar follow this three-way division, which matches the Arthashastra’s mandala theory of foreign relations. Most commentators add ‘through spies’ in brackets because the chapter context requires it, even though the word ஒற்று is not in the line. The closing தொழில் (‘occupation, duty’) presents knowing as the king’s trade and not something he does now and then. The wording is the same on all three sources consulted; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi form எல்லார்க்கு மெல்லா.

tamil:
ஒற்றினான் ஒற்றிப் பொருள்தெரியா மன்னவன்
கொற்றங் கொளக்கிடந்தது இல்.
transliteration:
Otrinaan otrip poruldheriyaa mannavan
Kotrang kolakkidandhadhu il.
current_meaning: A king who does not collect news through spies and understand what it means has no way to win.
elementary: Imagine a football coach who never watches the other team play and never thinks about what their moves mean. He will keep losing. This kural says a leader has to find out what is going on and then think carefully about what it means.
university: The first line repeats the root ஒற்று (ஒற்றினான் ஒற்றி, ‘spying by means of a spy’), a figure of repetition that runs through the whole chapter. The key phrase is பொருள் தெரியா, ‘not discerning the meaning or import’. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as not examining the benefit (பயன்) of what spies report, and Pulavar Kesikan as not working out the significance of events in enemy lands. So Valluvar is not satisfied with collecting data; the king must interpret it. The second line, கொற்றங் கொளக்கிடந்தது இல், says literally that ‘there is nothing lying there for him to take as victory’. Pappaiah widens கொற்றம் from battlefield victory to lasting success of the government. The text agrees on all three sources; thirukkural-thamizh.org prints ஒற்றினா னொற்றிப் பொருடெரியா, with the sandhi shown.

tamil:
வினைசெய்வார் தம்சுற்றம் வேண்டாதார் என்றாங்கு
அனைவரையும் ஆராய்வது ஒற்று.
transliteration:
Vinaiseyvaar thamsutram vaendaadhaar endraangu
Anaivaraiyum aaraaivadhu otru.
current_meaning: A true spy watches everyone without exception: the king’s own officers, his relatives, and his enemies too.
elementary: A fair referee watches every player on the field, even the ones from his own town and even his friends. If he only watched one team, the game would be unfair. This kural says a good investigator checks on everyone equally.
university: Valluvar names three groups: வினைசெய்வார் (those who carry out the king’s business, i.e. officials), தம் சுற்றம் (the king’s own kin), and வேண்டாதார் (those who do not wish him well, i.e. enemies). He then sums them up in அனைவரையும் (‘all of them’). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar take தம் to mean the king’s own relatives. Kalaignar reads the couplet as a rule of impartiality for the spy, who must not make exceptions for those he likes or dislikes. Pappaiah modernises the groups as civil servants, the ruling party, the opposition and foreigners, and says the spy reads their inner intent (மனக்கருத்து) from their words and deeds. The couplet is also a definition, ending ‘… is a spy’ (ஒற்று), a form repeated in 585-587. The text agrees across sources, with thirukkural-thamizh.org giving the sandhi form தஞ்சுற்றம்.

tamil:
கடாஅ உருவொடு கண்ணஞ்சாது யாண்டும்
உகாஅமை வல்லதே ஒற்று.
transliteration:
Kadaaa uruvodu kannanjaadhu yaandum
Ugaaamai valladhae otru.
current_meaning: A real spy looks ordinary so no one suspects him, does not get nervous when people stare, and never lets his secret slip anywhere.
elementary: In a game of hide-and-seek in plain sight, the best player looks totally ordinary, stays calm even when someone stares at them, and never giggles and gives themselves away. This kural says a good spy is like that: ordinary-looking, calm and able to keep a secret.
university: The couplet names three qualities, and two of its words use the lengthened vowel (அளபெடை): கடாஅ உரு, ‘a form that does not provoke questioning’ (from கடாவுதல், to interrogate), and உகாஅமை, ‘not spilling’ (from உகுத்தல், to let fall, i.e. to leak a secret). In between comes கண் அஞ்சாது, ‘not fearing the eyes’ of suspicious onlookers. Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as not fearing the looks of those who watch him. Pappaiah adds that the spy must hold out whatever method is used on him, naming the four upāyas (sāma, dāna, bheda, daṇḍa: persuasion, bribery, division, force). யாண்டும் (‘anywhere, at any time’) makes the secrecy absolute. The wording agrees across sources; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi கண்ணஞ்சா தியாண்டு முகாஅமை.

tamil:
துறந்தார் படிவத்த ராகி இறந்தாராய்ந்து
என்செயினும் சோர்விலது ஒற்று.
transliteration:
Thurandhaar padivaththa raagi irandhaaraaindhu
Enseyinum soarviladhu otru.
current_meaning: A good spy disguises himself as a holy man who has given up the world, goes into places no one else can, learns everything, and never gives himself away, whatever is done to him.
elementary: In old stories, a clever messenger sometimes dresses as a humble traveller so he can pass through the gates. Even if guards question him roughly, he stays in character and keeps his secret. This kural describes that kind of brave, patient spy.
university: துறந்தார் படிவத்தர் ஆகி means ‘taking on the form (படிவம்) of those who have renounced’, that is, dressing as an ascetic or wandering monk. Such figures could travel freely in ancient India. இறந்து ஆராய்ந்து is read by Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘going beyond [ordinary limits], into places otherwise unreachable, and examining’. Pappaiah makes it explicit: places one cannot go. என்செயினும் சோர்வு இலது means ‘whatever [the suspicious] may do to him, he does not slip’. Here சோர்வு means a lapse that gives the secret away, not tiredness, and Pappaiah and Kalaignar both read it as holding out under torture. The disguise matches the Arthashastra’s tāpasa (ascetic) spy closely, which is often cited in comparative studies of the Kural. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net give identical text; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi forms ராகி யிறந்தாராய்ந் / தென்செயினுஞ் சோர்வில தொற்று.

tamil:
மறைந்தவை கேட்கவற் றாகி அறிந்தவை
ஐயப்பாடு இல்லதே ஒற்று.
transliteration:
Maraindhavai kaetkavat raagi arindhavai
Aiyappaadu illadhae otru.
current_meaning: A spy is someone who can uncover hidden secrets and has no doubt at all about what he has found.
elementary: A good detective in a mystery story does two things: she finds the hidden clues, and she checks them until she is sure before she tells anyone. Guessing isn’t enough. This kural says a real investigator uncovers secrets and makes sure they are true.
university: மறைந்தவை கேட்க வற்று ஆகி means ‘being able (வற்று, ‘capable’) to hear what is concealed’. அறிந்தவை ஐயப்பாடு இல்லது means ‘having no doubt about what has been learned’. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the second half as being able to decide firmly without wavering. Pappaiah adds that the spy draws secrets ‘from the very mouth of those who did the deed’, and Kalaignar that he learns through those who are present at secret meetings. So the couplet sets two standards, access to secrets and certainty about them, and the next two couplets (588-589) add a check on that certainty from the king’s side. The text is identical across the three sources, apart from the sandhi யறிந்தவை / யையப்பா டில்லதே in thirukkural-thamizh.org.

tamil:
ஒற்றொற்றித் தந்த பொருளையும் மற்றுமோர்
ஒற்றினால் ஒற்றிக் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Otrotrith thandha porulaiyum matrumoar
Otrinaal otrik kolal.
current_meaning: Even news that a spy has brought in should be believed only after another spy has checked it.
elementary: If one friend tells you there is no school tomorrow, you would probably check with another friend or the school website before staying home. This kural says a wise leader always double-checks a report with a second source.
university: The couplet plays on the root ஒற்று, which appears four times (ஒற்று ஒற்றித் தந்த … ஒற்றினால் ஒற்றி): ‘what a spy has spied out and delivered, have it spied out again by another spy, and then accept it’. The உம் in பொருளையும் (‘even the information’) means that even a reliable spy’s report is not exempt. Mu. Varadarasanar says it should be taken as true only after the two accounts are found to agree (ஒப்புமை கண்டபின்). Kalaignar stresses comparing the two reports before deciding. கொளல் is an infinitive-style imperative (‘one should accept’), the same form Valluvar uses for maxims elsewhere. This couplet and 589 together set out a clear doctrine of corroborating intelligence. The text agrees across all three sources.

tamil:
ஒற்றெற் றுணராமை ஆள்க உடன்மூவர்
சொற்றொக்க தேறப் படும்.
transliteration:
Otret runaraamai aalga udanmoovar
Sotrokka thaerap padum.
current_meaning: Use spies so that none of them knows about the others. When three such spies report the same thing, you can believe it.
elementary: If three students are each asked separately what happened at recess, and they can’t talk to each other first, but all three tell the same story, the teacher can be pretty sure it is true. This kural says a wise leader checks the truth the same way.
university: The first line says to employ (ஆள்க) spies in a way that one does not become aware (உணராமை) of another. The second says that when the words of three (மூவர் சொல்) agree together (தொக்க), the thing may be trusted (தேறப்படும்). There is a real textual variant in the first word. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print ஒற்றெற் றுணராமை, while thirukkural-thamizh.org prints ஒற்றொற் றுணராமை, i.e. ஒற்று ஒற்று உணராமை, ‘one spy not knowing another spy’. That is the sense every commentator, including Parimelazhagar, gives, and the -எற்று form is best explained as a sandhi or scribal variant. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the second line as ‘if the three agree, take it as true’. Pappaiah is more cautious: even when three agree, examine it before accepting. The rule is strikingly close to Arthashastra 1.12, which requires agreement from three independent sources and says the spy-units must not know one another.

tamil:
சிறப்பறிய ஒற்றின்கண் செய்யற்க செய்யின்
புறப்படுத்தான் ஆகும் மறை.
transliteration:
Sirapariya otrinkan seyyarka seyyin
Purappaduththaan aagum marai.
current_meaning: A king should not reward a spy where others can see. If he does, he gives away his own secret.
elementary: Imagine a secret helper who quietly tells the teacher when someone is being picked on. If the teacher gave that helper a big prize in front of the whole class, everyone would know who the helper was, and the secret would be ruined. This kural says to thank secret helpers quietly.
university: சிறப்பு அறிய means ‘so that the honour is known [to others]’; ஒற்றின்கண் செய்யற்க, ‘do not do it to the spy’; செய்யின் புறப்படுத்தான் ஆகும் மறை, ‘if you do, you become the one who brought the secret out into the open (புறப்படுத்தல்)’. The irony is that after all the care in 585-589 to keep spies hidden, the king himself becomes the leak by rewarding them publicly. Pappaiah reads the couplet as ‘reward the spy, but reward him secretly’, which fits Sun Tzu’s and Kautilya’s view that spies must be generously paid. Mu. Varadarasanar reads மறை as both the secret information and the spy’s identity. The text agrees across sources; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi form வொற்றின்கட் செய்யற்க செய்யிற் / புறப்படுத்தா னாகு மறை.

tamil:
உடையர் எனப்படுவது ஊக்கம் அஃதில்லார்
உடையது உடையரோ மற்று.
transliteration:
