Inaroozhththum naaraa malaranaiyar katradhu
Unara viriththuraiyaa thaar.
current_meaning: People who cannot explain what they have learned so others understand it are like flowers that bloom in bunches but have no smell.
elementary: Imagine a bunch of beautiful flowers that have no smell at all: nice to look at, but something is missing. A person who knows a lot but can’t explain it to anyone is like that. Learning is meant to be shared.
university: The closing couplet uses an uvamai (simile): iṇar (a cluster or bunch) ūḻttum (though it blossoms) nāṟā malar (a flower that gives no scent). Kaṟṟatu uṇara virittu uraiyātār means those who do not expand (virittu) and state (urai) what they have learned so that others may grasp it (uṇara). Parimelazhagar’s point is that learning (kalvi), however full, is incomplete in a counsellor unless it can be communicated, which links this chapter back to ch. 40 (Kalvi) and ch. 42 (Kēḷvi). The texts differ on the first word: ytamizh.com prints இணருழ்த்தும் with a short u, and the older edition prints இணருழ்த்து நாறா; many standard editions have the expected long-vowel form இணரூழ்த்தும் (iṇar + ūḻttum). The older edition also divides the second line as கற்ற / துணர விரித்துரையா தார் for metre.

tamil:
துணைநலம் ஆக்கம் தரூஉம் வினைநலம்
வேண்டிய எல்லாந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Thunainalam aakkam tharooum vinainalam
Vendiya ellaan tharum.
current_meaning: Good helpers can bring a person success, but good actions bring everything a person could want.
elementary: Good friends can help you build a bigger sandcastle. But if you build it the right way, patiently and fairly, you get the castle, you keep your friends, and people want to play with you again. Doing things the right way gives you more than any helper can.
university: The chapter opens by ranking two kinds of nalam (goodness, excellence): tuṇai-nalam, the excellence of one’s supporters, the theme of the earlier chapter on seeking the help of the great (ch. 45), and vinai-nalam, the goodness or purity of the action itself, which gives the chapter its name, vinai-t-tūymai. Parimelazhagar reads ākkam narrowly as material increase, while vēṇṭiya ellām (all that is desired) takes in fame and merit in this world and the next, so good allies secure only one good while pure action secures all of them. The line sets the ethical frame for this part of the Amaichiyal (chapters on the minister, 64-73): a minister’s competence (ch. 64) and eloquence (ch. 65) are worthless unless the means he uses are clean. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah follow this contrast closely, while Kalaignar softens it into a partnership in which allies add strength and good deeds done with them bring every benefit. On the text: ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net both print த்ருஉம், an evident keying error. The sandhi-joined text at thirukkural-thamizh.org has தரூஉம் (tarūum, the alapeṭai lengthening of tarum), and that reading is adopted here.

tamil:
என்றும் ஒருவுதல் வேண்டும் புகழொடு
நன்றி பயவா வினை.
transliteration:
Endrum oruvudhal vendum pugazhodu
Nandri payavaa vinai.
current_meaning: Always stay away from any action that brings neither a good name nor any real good.
elementary: Before you do something, ask two questions: will people be proud of me for this, and will it truly help? If the answer to both is no, don’t do it, even if it looks easy or tempting.
university: The couplet gives the test that runs through the whole chapter: a deed must yield pukaḻ (fame, good name) together with naṉṟi (benefit, goodness), and a deed that yields neither is to be avoided (oruvutal, ‘setting aside, shunning’) at all times (eṉṟum). Parimelazhagar and later commentators such as Solomon Pappaiah read the pair as fame in this life and merit (aṟam) for the life to come, so a clean act must be both publicly honourable and morally fruitful. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the rejected deeds as those ‘without purity’ (tūymai aṟṟa), tying the verse to the chapter title. The prose explanation printed with Pope’s translation (‘acts which, in addition to fame, yield no benefit’) reads pukaḻoṭu slightly differently, but all readings agree that honour alone is not enough without real good. The text is stable across all three sources consulted.

tamil:
ஒஓதல் வேண்டும் ஒளிமாழ்கும் செய்வினை
ஆஅதும் என்னு மவர்.
transliteration:
Oodhal vendum olimaazhkum seyvinai
Aaadhum ennu mavar.
current_meaning: People who say 'we want to rise higher' must stay away from any action that would dim their good name.
elementary: If you want to become class captain, you wouldn’t cheat on a test, because once people see you cheat they stop trusting you. Anyone who wants to grow greater has to keep their good name bright and stay away from anything that would spoil it.
university: Two alapeṭai (metrical lengthenings) mark the couplet: ஒஓதல் for ஓதல்/ஒருவுதல் (avoiding, shunning), and ஆஅதும் for ஆதும், ‘we shall become (greater)’, which Parimelazhagar takes as the resolve of those who seek to rise ever higher. Oḷi (light, radiance) stands here for reputation and dignity, and oḷi-māḻkum seyviṉai means acts that cause that radiance to fade. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar both take oḷi as pukaḻ (fame), linking this verse to the fame-and-good test of 652, while Solomon Pappaiah reads it as ‘one’s standing in one’s own lifetime’. The logic is a statesman’s: ambition itself is a reason for scruple, since a stained name blocks the rise one hopes for. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree on the text; thirukkural-thamizh.org prints the sandhi-joined form ஒஓதல் வேண்டு மொளிமாழ்குஞ் செய்வினை / யாஅது மென்னு மவர்.

tamil:
இடுக்கண் படினும் இளிவந்த செய்யார்
நடுக்கற்ற காட்சி யவர்.
transliteration:
Idukkan padinum ilivandha seyyaar
Nadukkatra kaatchi yavar.
current_meaning: People who see clearly and are not shaken will never do anything shameful, even when they are in deep trouble.
elementary: Imagine you lost your lunch money and saw someone else’s wallet on the floor. A person with a steady, clear mind would still hand it in, even though they’re hungry. Being in trouble doesn’t make a wrong thing right.
university: Iṭukkaṇ is ‘distress, affliction’ (compare the chapter iṭukkaṇ aḻiyāmai, ch. 63), and iḷivanta means ‘what brings disgrace’. Parimelazhagar takes the past-tense participle literally as ‘acts that have (in the past) brought disgrace’, which is why the prose explanation printed with Pope says ‘acts which have brought disgrace (on former ministers)’. The key phrase naṭukku-aṟṟa kāṭci, ‘vision free of trembling’, describes firm, clear discernment that does not waver under pressure, and Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as ‘motionless, clear knowledge’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar add that such people will not act basely even to escape their distress, which prepares for the stronger case of 656. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net read இடுக்கண் படினும்; thirukkural-thamizh.org shows the sandhi form இடுக்கட் படினு மிளிவந்த.

tamil:
எற்றென்று இரங்குவ செய்யற்க செய்வானேல்
மற்றன்ன செய்யாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Etrendru iranguva seyyarka seyvaanel
Matranna seyyaamai nandru.
current_meaning: Do not do anything that will later make you cry, 'What have I done!' And if you have already done such a thing, it is best not to do it again.
elementary: If you ever do something that makes you think ‘Oh no, why did I do that?’, the best thing is to learn from it and never do it again. Even better is to stop and think first, so you don’t have to feel that way at all.
university: Eṟṟu eṉṟu is an exclamation of dismay (‘what is this!’), and iraṅkuva are deeds one will afterwards lament. The first line forbids such deeds, and the second deals with the case where one has already done one. Here the commentaries split. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read maṟṟu aṉṉa ceyyāmai as ‘not doing such things again’, so repentance means not repeating the fault. The older reading, kept in the Drew-Lazarus prose explanation printed with Pope (‘it were good that he grieved not’) and in Puliyur Kesikan, takes aṉṉa ceyyāmai as ‘not doing that (grieving) again’: a minister should not waste himself in useless regret. This reading is usually traced to Parimelazhagar. The text also varies: ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net read செய்வானேல் (‘if he does’), while thirukkural-thamizh.org prints செய்வானேன், probably a typographical variant, since the conditional -ēl is needed for the sense.

tamil:
ஈன்றாள் பசிகாண்பான் ஆயினுஞ் செய்யற்க
சான்றோர் பழிக்கும் வினை.
transliteration:
Eendraal pasikaanbaan aayinum seyyarka
Saandror pazhikkum vinai.
current_meaning: Even if you have to watch your own mother go hungry, do not do anything that wise people would call wrong.
elementary: Suppose someone you love very much needs help. You would want to do anything for them, but stealing or lying still isn’t the right way. The Kural says even love for your own mother doesn’t make a wrong deed right. You must find an honest way to help.
university: This is the strongest statement in the chapter. Īṉṟāḷ, ‘she who bore (you)’, is the mother; pacikāṇpāṉ āyiṉum means ‘even if he should (have to) see her hunger’. Tamil ethics counts care of parents among the highest duties, so the verse deliberately picks the hardest case: not even that duty justifies deeds the cāṉṟōr (people of perfected character) condemn. Parimelazhagar and the modern commentators read the line without exception clauses, and Kalaignar sharpens it to ‘not even to relieve’ her suffering. This contrasts with the Sanskrit doctrine of āpad-dharma (law in emergencies), where the Mahabharata allows the sage Vishvamitra, in famine, to steal dog’s flesh to survive. The Kural here refuses that concession. The text is identical across sources apart from the sandhi form பசிகாண்பா னாயினுஞ் in thirukkural-thamizh.org. (Solomon Pappaiah’s printed gloss has பெற்றவனின், apparently a slip for பெற்றவளின்.)

tamil:
பழிமலைந்து எய்திய ஆக்கத்தின் சான்றோர்
கழிநல் குரவே தலை.
transliteration:
Pazhimalaindhu eydhiya aakkaththin saandror
Kazhinal kuravae thalai.
current_meaning: For good people, being very poor is better than getting rich in a shameful way.
elementary: Would you rather have a small lunch you paid for honestly, or a big feast you got by cheating? The Kural says the small honest lunch is worth far more, because you can enjoy it with a clear heart.
university: Paḻi malaintu, ‘having taken on / worn blame’ (malai- as in wearing a garland), describes wealth won by accepting disgrace, and ākkattiṉ is the comparative ablative, ‘than such wealth’. Kaḻi nalkuravu is ‘extreme, excessive poverty’ (kaḻi = beyond measure). Parimelazhagar takes it as the poverty of the cāṉṟōr, and Mu. Varadarasanar adds that they accept it because they keep purity of action (viṉait-tūymai). Talai means ‘head, foremost’, so such poverty ranks first. The couplet restates 656 as a general value judgement and prepares for the fate of tainted wealth in 658-660. All three sources agree on the text; thirukkural-thamizh.org shows the sandhi forms மலைந் தெய்திய வாக்கத்திற்.

tamil:
கடிந்த கடிந்தொரார் செய்தார்க்கு அவைதாம்
முடிந்தாலும் பீழை தரும்.
transliteration:
Kadindha kadindhoraar seydhaarkku avaidhaam
Mudindhaalum peezhai tharum.
current_meaning: People who do the things the wise have told them not to do will suffer for it, even if those things work out.
elementary: If you sneak a cookie from the jar after being told not to, you might get the cookie, but then you feel worried and guilty, and you might get caught later. Even when a wrong plan ‘works’, it ends up making you unhappy.
university: The first line plays on the verb kaṭi- (‘forbid, reject’): kaṭinta, ‘things forbidden (by the great)’, and kaṭintu orār, ‘those who do not reject them and turn away’. Solomon Pappaiah specifies that such people act ‘thinking to gather wealth’, keeping the chapter’s focus on means of gain. The concessive muṭintālum, ‘even if they are accomplished’, is the point: success does not clean a forbidden act, which still brings pīḻai (suffering, affliction). Parimelazhagar’s tradition takes the suffering to come in this life as well as the next, through loss of reputation and later retribution. All sources agree on the text; thirukkural-thamizh.org divides it as செய்தார்க் கவைதா / முடிந்தாலும்.

tamil:
அழக்கொண்ட எல்லாம் அழப்போம் இழப்பினும்
பிற்பயக்கும் நற்பா லவை.
transliteration:
Azhakkonda ellaam azhappoam izhappinum
Pirpayakkum narpaa lavai.
current_meaning: Everything gained by making others cry will be lost and leave you crying. Things gained in good ways may be lost for a while, but they will pay off later.
elementary: If you take a toy by making another child cry, that toy will bring you trouble and tears in the end. But if you get something fairly and then lose it, good things will still come back to you later.
university: The first line hinges on the double use of aḻa, ‘so as to weep’: what was taken (koṇṭa) while making others weep will depart (pōm) making the taker weep. It is a compact statement of moral retribution. The second line balances it: naṟ-pālavai, ‘things of a good kind’, meaning wealth obtained by fair means, even if lost (iḻappiṉum), will give fruit afterwards (piṟ-payakkum). Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah read this ‘fruit’ as a return of benefit in this life or merit in the next, and Kalaignar says such wealth ‘comes back again’. The verse sharpens the chapter’s theme of means into a law of consequences. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi form அழக்கொண்ட வெல்லா மழப்போ மிழப்பினும் / பிற்பயக்கு நற்பா லவை.

tamil:
சலத்தால் பொருள்செய்தே மார்த்தல் பசுமண்
கலத்துள்நீர் பெய்திரீஇ யற்று.
transliteration:
Salaththaal porulseydhe maarththal pasuman
Kalaththulneer peydhireei yatru.
current_meaning: Trying to keep yourself safe with money gained by cheating is like pouring water into a pot of wet, unbaked clay and hoping it holds.
elementary: If you pour water into a pot made of wet, unbaked clay, the pot softens and falls apart, and the water leaks away. Money gained by cheating is like that: it seems to hold for a moment, but it melts away and takes the ‘pot’ with it.
university: Calam means deceit or crooked means, and poruḷ ceytu ēmārttal (sandhi ceytē mārttal) is ‘to make wealth and guard/secure (with it)’, from ēmam, safety or protection. Parimelazhagar reads the verse in its ministerial setting: a minister who tries to protect his king and realm with wealth gained by fraud. This is why the prose explanation printed with Pope says ‘(For a minister) to protect (his king)’. The image is pacu-maṇ kalam, a pot of green, unfired clay: pouring water in and trying to keep it there (peytu irīi, with irīi an alapeṭai of iruttal, ‘to keep’) destroys both the water and the vessel. The metaphor makes the same point as the rest of the chapter: foul means undo themselves and ruin the very thing they were meant to protect. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree on the text; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi forms சலத்தாற் … பசுமட் / கலத்துணீர்.

tamil:
வினைத்திட்பம் என்பது ஒருவன் மனத்திட்பம்
மற்றைய எல்லாம் பிற.
transliteration:
Vinaiththitpam enpadhu oruvan manaththitpam
Matraiya ellaam piRa.
current_meaning: Being firm in action really means being firm in mind. Every other kind of strength is something different.
elementary: Imagine two kids building a tall block tower. Both have the same blocks, but one gives up when it wobbles and the other keeps going. The blocks are not what made the difference. The strong part was inside the kid who kept going. That inside strength is what gets things done.
university: The chapter title vinai-t-tiṭpam pairs vinai (undertaking, action) with tiṭpam (solidity, firmness), and the opening couplet at once relocates that firmness from the deed to the doer: vinai-t-tiṭpam is maṉa-t-tiṭpam, firmness of mind. Parimelazhagar glosses maṟṟaiya ellām (all the others) as the external supports a minister or king might count on, such as army, fortifications, wealth and allies, and says these are piṟa, other things, not what is meant by the word. The chapter follows directly on vinai-t-tūymai (ch. 66, purity of means), so the Amaichiyal sequence runs: choose clean means, then carry them through with an unshaken mind. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah follow this reading closely (Pappaiah: the resolve not to abandon a task midway), while Kalaignar turns it conditionally: whatever else one has, without firmness of mind there is no firmness in action. The text is identical in ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net and the sandhi-joined edition at thirukkural-thamizh.org.

tamil:
ஊறொரால் உற்றபின் ஒல்காமை இவ்விரண்டின்
ஆறென்பர் ஆய்ந்தவர் கோள்.
transliteration:
OoRoraal utrapin olkaamai ivviraNdin
AaRenpar aaindhavar koaL.
current_meaning: People who have studied this say firm action follows two rules: stay away from harm before it comes, and do not give up when it comes anyway.
elementary: Before riding your bike, you check the tyres and wear a helmet so you don’t get hurt. But if you still fall, you don’t quit biking forever; you get up and keep riding. Being careful first, and being brave after, are the two secrets of finishing things.
university: The couplet sets out a two-part rule: ūṟu orāl, keeping clear of harm (ūṟu, injury or obstacle; orāl, avoidance), and uṟṟa piṉ olkāmai, not flagging (olku, to shrink or slacken) once harm has struck. Parimelazhagar reads the first clause as not undertaking an act likely to come to grief, and the ‘āyntavar’ (those who have investigated) as the authors of the political treatises (nīti nūl), so that the couplet cites a consensus of statecraft; Solomon Pappaiah follows him. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar instead read the first clause as removing an obstacle before it arrives, which puts more weight on foresight than on choice of task. Either way, firmness is shown to include prudence, not mere stubbornness, which links this chapter back to terintu ceyal vakai (ch. 47). The three web texts agree on the wording.

tamil:
கடைக்கொட்கச் செய்தக்க தாண்மை இடைக்கொட்கின்
எற்றா விழுமந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Kadaikkotkach seydhakka thaaNmai idaikkotkin
Etraa vizhumanh tharum.
current_meaning: Real skill means keeping a task quiet until it is finished. If people learn about it halfway, it can cause trouble that cannot be fixed.
elementary: If you are making a surprise birthday card for your mom and you show it to her half-done, the surprise is ruined and you can’t get it back. It is better to work quietly and show it when it’s finished. Some plans work best when they are kept secret until they are done.
university: The key verb is koṭku, to become manifest: kaṭai-k-koṭka, so that it appears at the end, versus iṭai-k-koṭkiṉ, if it appears in the middle. Āṇmai is literally ‘manliness’ but here means competence or mastery in execution (Solomon Pappaiah renders it āḷumai, capability), and eṟṟā vizhumam is sorrow that cannot be removed. Parimelazhagar explains that a plan disclosed before completion lets enemies obstruct it, so secrecy is part of firmness; Kalaignar makes the point explicitly, calling concealment till completion the very ‘firmness of execution’. This couplet echoes the Arthashastra tradition on the secrecy of counsel (mantra-rakṣā) and anticipates the chapter on the conduct of affairs (ch. 68). Some readers print the first line with sandhi, ceytakkatāṇmai; the three sources consulted agree on the wording.

tamil:
சொல்லுதல் யார்க்கும் எளிய அரியவாம்
சொல்லிய வண்ணம் செயல்.
transliteration:
Solludhal yaarkkum eLiya ariyavaam
Solliya vaNNam seyal.
current_meaning: Anyone can talk about how to do something. The hard part is doing it exactly the way it was said.
elementary: It is easy to say, “I will clean my whole room today!” It is much harder to actually pick up every sock and toy. Anyone can make a promise; the strong person is the one who does what they said.
university: The couplet balances eḷiya (easy) against ariya (hard, rare), and solludal (saying) against solliya vaṇṇam seyal (acting in the manner that was said). Parimelazhagar takes solludal as stating how a task ought to be carried out, the counsel a minister gives, so the couplet sets planning and advice against execution; Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan follow him, while Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar widen it to any promise or declaration. The plural eḷiya / ariya (literally ‘easy things’, ‘hard things’) is idiomatic and is normally rendered in the singular. In the chapter’s argument the couplet explains why firmness of mind is needed at all: plans are cheap, and only a firm mind turns word into deed. All three sources agree on the text.

tamil:
வீறெய்தி மாண்டார் வினைத்திட்பம் வேந்தன்கண்
ஊறெய்தி உள்ளப் படும்.
transliteration:
VeeReydhi maaNdaar vinaiththitpam vaendhankaN
OoReydhi uLLap padum.
current_meaning: The firm action of people who have become great reaches even the king, and so everyone comes to respect it.
elementary: When a student works hard and finishes a great project, the teacher notices, then the principal hears about it, and soon the whole school knows. Steady, finished work travels up to the people in charge, and everyone respects it.
university: Vīṟu is distinction or excellence and māṇṭār those who are great or eminent; the verb māḷ can also mean ‘to die’, and Sivayogi Sivakumar’s gloss on ytamizh.com reads the phrase as ‘those who died valiantly’, but the mainstream commentators (Parimelazhagar, Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar, Puliyur Kesikan) take māṇṭār as ‘the eminent’. Parimelazhagar specifies that their eminence comes from excellence of counsel (eṇṇam), and that their firmness in execution, by ‘reaching’ the king (vēntaṉkaṇ ūṟu eyti, where ūṟu means contact or effect, not harm as in 662), is then esteemed by everyone (uḷḷappaṭum). The couplet thus explains how a minister’s firmness is rewarded: it becomes visible through the ruler’s regard. Pope’s ‘With king acceptance finds and fame through all the state’ follows the same reading. The three sources agree on the text.
